sentences.text: Efraasia was a lightly built, medium-sized sauropodomorph dinosaur featuring graceful hands and feet relative to its body size.
This animal possessed a small, pointed, triangular skull with four teeth in the premaxilla and a moderately elongated but slender neck.
The skeleton displays two unique autapomorphies: a raised crescent-like ridge on the inner pubis shaft and a vaulted bony web between braincase extensions with a central platform.
Von Huene identified gastroliths associated with specimen SMNS 12667, suggesting Efraasia swallowed stones to aid digestion.

Master mason Albert Burrer began exploiting the Weiße Steinbruch quarry near Pfaffenhofen in Württemberg in 1902 and donated his findings to paleontologist Professor Fraas of the königliche Stuttgarter Naturalienkabinett from 1906 until the quarry closed in 1914.

Initially, Friedrich von Huene placed Efraasia in the genus Teratosaurus in 1908 because its bones were mixed with a Rauisuchia reptile, but Eberhard Fraas discovered the initial error, retained the name for the jaw, and erected the genus Efraasia.
Friedrich von Huene described the first specimen of Efraasia in 1907–1908, originally naming it Teratosaurus minor.
Adam Yates published a comprehensive study on Efraasia fossils in 2003.

Efraasia likely exhibited facultative bipedalism, capable of walking on both two and four legs, a trait shared by many primitive sauropodomorphs that may have been partially bipedal and partially quadrupedal.
Efraasia possessed long fingers and mobile thumbs adapted for grasping food, while its wrist structure may have facilitated quadrupedal locomotion or allowed easy quadrupedal walking.
Efraasia was a herbivore that lived approximately 210 million years ago during the Late Triassic in what is now Germany.
Efraasia minor is the only known species of the extinct genus Efraasia, a prosauropod sauropodomorph dinosaur that lived during the Late Triassic in Europe.
In 1965, Charig reclassified Efraasia as a plant-eating sauropodomorph.

Modern phylogenetic analysis places Efraasia as a basal sauropodomorph, more derived than Thecodontosaurus but less derived than Prosauropoda or Sauropoda, and is considered a primitive sauropodomorph that is more advanced than Thecodontosaurus but less advanced than prosauropods like Plateosaurus or early sauropods like Anchisaurus.
Efraasia was found in Germany in the Lowenstein Formation in Baden-Wurttemberg, and the fossil-bearing stratum was part of the Stubensandstein member of the Lower Löwenstein Formation.
Efraasia lived during the Norian stage, from 227.3 to 205.7 million years ago.

Some researchers debate whether Efraasia was an obligate biped, arguing that its lower arm anatomy prevented pronation and downward-facing hands, while others argue that Efraasia's lower arm structure prevented pronation, forcing it to be an obligate biped.
